title: Calming and seeing
hookLine: Zhiyi's meditation manual of stopping and seeing

lines: REST THE FEET, THEN THE EYES WORK.
cards: Three words painted on a sign at a railroad crossing, and kids learn them in that order. Not look, then stop.

You can't really look while you're still running; the feet have to come to rest before the eyes can do their work. A monk on a Chinese mountain built a whole meditation teaching on a pair of words that work the same way.
First you stop. Then you see. His teaching on it comes down in a long work and a short one, and students still sit with them.

teach.b: Zhi means stopping, or calming: the mind settling, the way a stirred-up glass of pond water goes still and the silt sinks. Guan means seeing, or contemplation: looking clearly at what's there once the water has cleared.
Behind the Chinese pair stand two older Indian words for the same practices, shamatha and vipashyana.

teach.h: A GREAT BOOK AND A SMALL ONE.
teach.b: Zhiyi's great meditation work, recorded by his student, is called Mohe Zhiguan, the great calming and seeing. It is long and demanding.
Tradition also gives him a short manual, often called the small calming and seeing, written for beginners, and it's surprisingly practical.
Before any talk of truths, it talks about adjusting your eating and your sleep, how to sit down and how to get up again, how to breathe so the breath is neither rough nor held.
Zhiyi doesn't treat the two as separate hobbies, calming some days and seeing on others. Stopping without seeing, the tradition warns, can turn dull and sleepy.
Seeing without stopping turns scattered, a flashlight swinging around a dark room. Together they steady each other. And what does the seeing actually see?

teach.h: THE SEEING FINDS THE THREE TRUTHS.
teach.b: In Tiantai, it looks into a single moment of mind and finds the three truths there: empty, provisional, and the middle.
So the stopping isn't the goal. It's the stillness that lets the seeing happen, the feet coming to rest at the crossing so the eyes can do their work.

how: Tiantai and Tendai practitioners train in calming and contemplation together, often beginning with Zhiyi's practical advice on posture, breath, food and sleep before turning to contemplation of the mind.

games.q: you've been sitting calmly for a while and you're starting to nod off. what does the tradition say to do?
o: turn to seeing: look clearly at what's here.
games.why: stopping without seeing turns dull. the seeing wakes it up, and the stopping keeps the seeing from scattering.

practice: Settle your body the way the small manual says, not slumped, not stiff, the breath smooth and unforced, and for the first stretch only stop, resting on the breath while the silt settles.
When things feel a little clearer, start to look at what's here, a sound, an ache, a passing thought, plainly, without chasing it. If you get scattered, stop again; if you get sleepy, look again.

wordCard.voice: Zhiguan. Stopping and seeing: calming the mind and looking clearly, practiced together as Zhiyi taught them. Today's word.
